lessons.title: SSRI-associated hyponatremia / possible SIADH
lessons.opening: An older patient taking sertraline and a diuretic develops new weakness and unsteadiness. What medication-related risk belongs in your differential?
facts: SSRIs can cause hyponatremia, often associated with SIADH. Older age, diuretic use and volume depletion raise risk. Symptomatic hyponatremia requires stopping sertraline and appropriate medical intervention.
gaps: Do not diagnose SIADH from medication exposure alone. Full diagnostic criteria and correction protocols are not loaded.

lessons.opening: A patient with type 2 diabetes and eGFR 28 has a new metformin order. Identify the issue; how would your reasoning differ at eGFR 40?

lessons.title: Metformin and iodinated contrast
lessons.opening: A metformin-treated patient with eGFR 50 is scheduled for iodinated contrast. What does this product label require?
facts: Hold at/before contrast for eGFR 30–60, relevant liver disease/alcoholism/heart failure history, or intra-arterial contrast. Recheck eGFR after 48 hours and restart if stable.
gaps: This is the product-label rule; radiology guidance may differ. Do not claim all sources agree or that every contrast exposure requires a hold.

lessons.title: Spironolactone with potassium-raising therapy
lessons.opening: A heart failure patient takes spironolactone, an ACE inhibitor and a potassium supplement. How do you assess safety without calling every combination absolutely contraindicated?
facts: Potassium-raising agents increase hyperkalemia risk. Spironolactone requires early and ongoing potassium monitoring; pre-existing hyperkalemia is contraindicated.
gaps: Combination decisions require indication, renal function, potassium and monitoring capacity. Do not invent a universal stop threshold.

lessons.title: Confusion, falls and polypharmacy
lessons.opening: A 76-year-old woman with depression, hypertension and osteoarthritis has new unsteadiness and difficulty concentrating. Sertraline was recently increased; she also takes a diuretic and uses OTC pain remedies. She lives alone. Give a one-sentence problem representation and identify the first safety concern.
reveals: After the initial differential: simulated sodium is 124 mmol/L; glucose 106 mg/dL.
After discussing next tests: baseline sodium was 138 one month earlier; oral intake has been poor. Serum/urine osmolality and volume assessment are not yet available.
Before the plan: she prioritizes staying independent and has difficulty arranging transportation.
facts: Sertraline-associated hyponatremia is a source-supported possible contributor; the case does not establish SIADH or exclude other causes.
gaps: Full hyponatremia differential, diagnostic thresholds and treatment protocols need additional evidence. No correction-rate teaching from this case.

lessons.title: Kidney function decline with competing chronic treatments
lessons.opening: A 68-year-old man with diabetes, hypertension and CKD reports poor intake and new dizziness. His list includes metformin, lisinopril, a diuretic and recently added OTC ibuprofen. What links these details, and what needs attention first?
reveals: After the differential: simulated creatinine is 2.3 mg/dL compared with 1.2 previously; current reported eGFR is 28.
After test planning: he is still taking all listed medicines and cannot name the OTC doses.
Before the plan: he fears losing blood pressure control if medicines are changed and has limited access to repeat laboratory testing.
facts: Medication exposure and volume depletion may contribute; do not assume a single cause. Metformin renal restrictions and the ACE inhibitor/NSAID warning are loaded.
gaps: A full AKI diagnostic/management guideline is not loaded. eGFR during changing renal function requires caution; do not turn the value into an automated dose calculator.

lessons.title: Fatigue and possible bleeding during anticoagulation
lessons.opening: An 82-year-old woman with nonvalvular AF, CKD and arthritis reports new fatigue and easy bruising. She takes apixaban and recently added OTC ibuprofen. How do you prioritize the differential and immediate assessment?
reveals: After initial assessment: simulated weight is 58 kg and serum creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL; she reports taking apixaban 5 mg twice daily.
After discussing tests: simulated hemoglobin is 8.6 g/dL compared with 12.0 previously; she then reports dark stools.
Before the plan: she strongly fears another stroke and is worried about medication costs.
facts: Reconcile the anticoagulant indication and AF reduction criteria. Medication risks do not by themselves prove the bleeding source.
gaps: GI bleeding diagnosis, transfusion thresholds, interruption/reversal and restarting anticoagulation require additional guideline evidence. Prioritize escalation reasoning without inventing a protocol.

lessons.title: Heart failure, CKD and a complicated medication transition
lessons.opening: A 70-year-old man with reduced-ejection-fraction heart failure, hypertension and CKD brings conflicting medication lists after a care transition. Lisinopril, spironolactone, potassium supplements and a new sacubitril/valsartan order all appear. What must you clarify before recommending a plan?
reveals: After reconciliation: he took lisinopril this morning and has not started the new prescription.
After targeted testing: simulated potassium is 5.4 mEq/L and eGFR is 38.
Before the plan: he cannot afford frequent laboratory visits and wants the simplest workable schedule.
facts: The ACE inhibitor/ARNI transition and potassium-raising therapy require separate safety assessments. Avoid treating every combination as an absolute contraindication.
gaps: Comprehensive heart failure sequencing, emergency potassium management and sacubitril/valsartan dosing need additional evidence.
